assessment.nobel_worthiness: Predicting the quantum spin Hall effect and the Z2 time-reversal-invariant topological insulator, then observing the helical edge channels in HgTe quantum wells, opened a new class of quantum matter. It is clear, original and tied to measured transport and spectroscopy, and theory and experiment match quantitatively. The 2016 prize covered topological phase transitions and the quantum Hall precursors, so this is a natural, distinct continuation.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical prediction and the Z2 classification. Molenkamp's group delivered the first experimental realization in HgTe wells, following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang are not in the credited list, so the trio is a fair but imperfect configuration. Three-dimensional topological insulators (Fu, Kane, Mele; Moore and Balents) are a related strand that may complicate credit.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with nearly two decades of independent confirmation, ARPES evidence for 3D topological insulators and widespread follow-on work. Timing is right and the interpretation is stable.
uncertainties: Credit for the HgTe proposal (Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang) falls outside the credited names.
Whether the prize should centre on 2D quantum spin Hall or 3D topological insulators is unresolved.
Practical device impact is limited so far.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Moire flat bands in magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene produced correlated insulators, superconductivity and later fractional Chern insulators in a clean, tunable platform. This is a field-defining discovery of new quantum behaviour in a 2D material, and it follows the graphene tradition recognized in 2010.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald predicted the flat bands and the magic angle. Jarillo-Herrero's group discovered the correlated insulator and superconducting phases (2018). Cao and others who did the experimental work are not in the credited list. The theory plus experiment pairing supports a fair three-person prize, with possible competing claims from earlier moire band-structure work (e.g. Lopes dos Santos, Peres, Castro Neto).
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and understood in broad outline, but the origin of the superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated. Some may call it premature, though the field's impact is exceptional.
uncertainties: The microscopic mechanism of superconductivity is unsettled.
Earlier theory by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto is outside the credited list.
Sample-dependent variability affects reproducibility.
Possible premature recognition.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realized Hubbard models with controlled parameters, showing the superfluid to Mott insulator transition and enabling quantum simulation of many-body matter. The work is original, clear and has lasting impact on condensed-matter questions, and it links quantitatively to theory.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch and Zoller proposed the Bose-Hubbard realization, Greiner and Bloch demonstrated the Mott transition and developed the toolbox, Esslinger led fermionic work and Cirac contributed to theory. Choosing three of five is contentious. Jaksch is not in the list.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with two decades of independent confirmation across many groups. The 2001 BEC and 2012 quantum-systems prizes partly overlap, which may count against it.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2001 and 2012 prizes.
The five-name credit list cannot be reduced to three without disputing the others.
The simulation-versus-computation framing is broad.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The prediction and experimental discovery of the quantum anomalous Hall effect gave quantized Hall conductance without an external magnetic field, a clear and verified topological quantum phenomenon with metrological implications. It is a conceptually elegant link between theory and measurement.
assessment.attribution: Fang, Dai and collaborators predicted the effect in Cr- or Fe-doped Bi2Te3 family materials (Science 2010), and Xue's group first observed it in 2013. Haldane's 1988 model is the conceptual root and is outside the credited list. Chang and others on the experimental team are not listed.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by several groups, but the quantization temperatures remain low and the best precision is still being improved. Reasonably mature but some further consolidation would be welcome.
uncertainties: Haldane's earlier model is not in the credited list.
Experimental team credit within Xue's group.
Low operating temperatures limit practical impact.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Current-induced spin-orbit torques allow electrical switching of magnetization without a spin-polarized current, underlying SOT-MRAM and efficient spintronics. It joins a fundamental interplay of spin-orbit coupling and magnetism with real device impact, an area I know well from magnetization-dynamics theory.
assessment.attribution: Miron and Gambardella demonstrated Rashba-type SOT switching in Pt/Co/AlOx (2011), and Buhrman demonstrated spin-Hall torque switching (2012). Spin Hall effect theory (Dyakonov, Hirsch and others) and the Rashba-Edelstein mechanism complicate credit, and the physical origin of the torque, bulk spin Hall versus interface Rashba, has been a long dispute.
assessment.maturity: Mature in industry terms, with widespread independent confirmation. The scientific interpretation, with interface versus bulk contributions, is still evolving, which makes the physics less clean than the technology.
uncertainties: Spin Hall and Rashba origins are disputed.
Foundational theory contributors are not in the credited list.
A device-driven prize may look more like engineering to some members.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks reached fractional uncertainties near 10^-18 and enable tests of fundamental physics, relativistic geodesy and a potential redefinition of the second. Katori's magic-wavelength idea and Ye's demonstrations of record stability are clear, original and quantitatively verified. The work is outside my own subfield, so I defer somewhat to colleagues in AMO physics.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock concept and Ye's group delivered the key precision milestones. A two-person prize is clean. Hall and Hansch were recognized in 2005 for the comb, and ion-clock pioneers (Wineland in 2012) are a nearby area.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed across several laboratories, with consistent comparisons of independent clocks. Highly mature, and recognition is timely given the coming redefinition of the second.
uncertainties: Overlap with earlier prizes on frequency combs and ion clocks.
Redefinition of the second has not yet occurred.
My own expertise in precision metrology is limited.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Subpicosecond demagnetization by femtosecond laser pulses and all-optical magnetic switching opened ultrafast magnetism, and they link directly to my own research on spin dynamics and the ERC Synergy-type questions on ultrafast correlated dynamics. The discovery is original and has had large impact on how we think about spin angular-momentum transfer.
assessment.attribution: Beaurepaire, Merle, Daunois and Bigot reported ultrafast demagnetization in nickel in 1996, so Bigot is a conspicuous omission. Kimel and Rasing showed non-thermal optical control of magnetization, and Stanciu, Hansteen and others discovered helicity-dependent all-optical switching. The credit is contested and the list leaves out important names. I may be biased by my own field, and a fair three-person prize is hard.
assessment.maturity: Many independent confirmations exist, but the microscopic mechanism of ultrafast demagnetization (spin-flip scattering, superdiffusive transport, others) is not settled, which makes the discovery less mature than topological or moire work.
uncertainties: Credit for the 1996 discovery involves Bigot, who is not credited.
Mechanism of ultrafast demagnetization is unresolved.
Possible conflict of interest through my own research programme.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum error-correcting codes and fault-tolerant computation showed that large-scale quantum computation is possible in principle, and topological codes inform current hardware. The ideas are original and foundational. The 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits relates to the hardware side of this field.
assessment.attribution: Shor and Steane independently found the first quantum error-correcting codes, and Kitaev introduced the toric code and anyon-based fault tolerance. Calderbank, Gottesman, Knill, Laflamme and Aharonov-Ben-Or (threshold theorem) also made decisive contributions, so three people leave out important contributors. Whether this belongs to physics versus computer science is a further question.
assessment.maturity: Theory is well accepted and early experimental demonstrations of below-threshold error correction are appearing, but a full practical realization is not yet verified, so recognition may be somewhat early. This is far from my own area of materials theory.
uncertainties: Credit is spread among many contributors outside the credited list.
Experimental confirmation of scalable error correction is still emerging.
Boundary of physics versus information theory.
